transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-04 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Leah Kim (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Auriga Head of Platform), Priya Rao (Auriga SRE), Evan Liu (Auriga CTO), Marta Gomez (Auriga Legal)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
Samir kicked off with goals: show org/project key patterns for multi-tenant rate policies, demonstrate console controls for quotas, and discuss a short dedicated pilot. Leah ran a quick demo of the console rate policy pages, sticky routing and fallback flows. Customer asked detailed Qs about SSO, KMS, and audit logs; legal requested SOC2 evidence. Agreed to a trial and to share playbook.

Topics covered:
- Org vs project key design patterns
- Rate limiting (token-per-minute, concurrency, burst)
- Quotas, fairshare and splits across teams
- Dedicated pools and sticky routing/fallbacks
- Security: KMS, encryption, audit logs, SSO/SAML, data residency
- Pilot scope, benchmarking and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I see we have the Auriga core platform folks, perfect. Quick intro, I'm Samir, AE at Redwood, with Leah our SE. Uh, what's the best goal you want to get out of this session?

[00:14] Carlos: Hi all, thanks. For us, top line is we need a playbook for org vs project keys — like where to put quotas, how to do bursts for interactive features vs batch, and questions about dedicated vs hosted. Also security expectations for enterprise.

[00:29] Samir: Perfect. That's exactly what we planned. Leah will run the console demo and then we can dig into policy patterns.

[00:39] Leah: Cool. I'll share screen — bear with me, slow network. So here's the Redwood Console, top nav, model routes. This is the rate policy page; you can create policies scoped to organization, project, or API key.

[00:55] Evan: Quick clarification — when you say project key are these per-tenant keys inside our single org, or is it multiple orgs?

[01:05] Leah: Good question. In your deployment you'd typically have one Redwood org representing Auriga account. Within that, project keys map to product lines or teams — e.g., "search", "inference-batch", "chat-ui" — those keys are attached to usage and quotas. You can set org-wide defaults and then override per-project.

[01:28] Priya: How do you handle fairshare? We have spikes where one team can blow past others.

[01:36] Leah: We have a couple of levers: concurrency limits per key, token-rate quotas (tokens/minute), and a fairshare policy that does proportional throttling when the pool is saturated. The console shows a visual of current allocation and allows weights per project.

[01:53] Samir: To add, for latency-sensitive routes we recommend low concurrency + reserved slots in a dedicated pool, while batch jobs can have higher concurrency but lower priority.

[02:06] Carlos: What about burst behavior? We sometimes need short bursts for interactive sessions.

[02:12] Leah: We support a token-bucket style burst allowance. You can set a burst window (e.g., allow 5x baseline for 30s) combined with a refill rate. Also there is sticky routing so burst traffic can route to a warmed instance or a higher tier pool when needed.

[02:28] Evan: Is sticky routing automatic or do we tag endpoints?

[02:33] Leah: Automatic by policy — you can designate route-level preferences: prefer-dedicated, prefer-hosted-cheapest, or latency-first. If preferred pool is full, fallback policies kick in. There was a slight delay in the console earlier — apologies, mm — new UI on my side.

[02:48] Priya: Ok, can we pin critical routes to dedicated capacity and use hosted for everything else?

[02:55] Samir: Exactly. Many customers do that: critical low-latency inference on Dedicated, and lower-cost batched embeddings on Hosted. We'll show how to configure that.

[03:10] Leah: Jumping back to the console demo — creating a rate policy: scope = project key, limit = 2000 tokens/min, concurrency = 8, burst = 10k tokens for 45s, fallback = "route to hosted-lower-cost". You can also attach quotas that reset monthly or daily.

[03:33] Carlos: Where do account-level quotas live? We want org-level spend caps so teams can't overspend.

[03:40] Leah: There's an org-level budget guard. You can set soft and hard caps. Soft cap emits alerts and can throttle non-critical routes automatically; hard cap will block further requests. We can also pipe alerts into your PagerDuty.

[03:56] Marta: Legal question — how granular is the audit logging? We need per-request traces for compliance.

[04:03] Leah: We keep audit logs for control plane actions and per-token request logs can be routed to your logging bucket in VPC mode. For hosted customers we retain request metadata for 30 days by default; in Private deployments you control retention.

[04:18] Marta: And encryption at rest / KMS?

[04:22] Samir: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS for private deployments and support BYOK — bring your own keys. Hosted has Redwood-managed keys, but you can opt into a dedicated key when on an enterprise agreement.

[04:36] Evan: Can we get a SOC2 package?

[04:39] Samir: Absolutely. We'll share SOC2 artifacts and the security whitepaper after the call.

[04:46] Priya: For pilot sizing, what metrics do you need from us?

[04:51] Leah: A 7-day traffic profile is ideal: requests per route, token distribution, average/max concurrency, and SLOs (p99 latency targets). Then we'll recommend a pool size and batching settings.

[05:06] Samir: Also, tell us about any regulatory constraints — data residency, region locks — that affects routing.

[05:15] Carlos: Europe only for some data, yes. We will provide region-by-region breakdown.

[05:21] Leah: Good. On the topic of billing segmentation: project keys can be tagged to different cost centers; the console exports token/billing breakdown per key. That helps for internal chargeback.

[05:36] Evan: Is there any way to do graceful degradation? Say the Dedicated pool is down, can we route to a cheaper fallback but with different model?

[05:44] Leah: Yes — fallback policies can point to model variants (e.g., gpt-medium vs gpt-large), lower-cost hosts, or queue requests with lower concurrency. You can set automatic rollbacks if quality metrics drop below threshold.

[05:59] Carlos: Curious about per-API key rate trimming — we want to give internal users generous limits but third-party integrators tighter ones.

[06:07] Leah: That's the typical pattern: org-level defaults, then project key overrides. Third-party integrator keys are in their own project with stricter quotas and an enforced SLA.

[06:20] Priya: Any gotchas with multi-tenant keys and caching? We do a lot of prefix reuse.

[06:26] Leah: We do prefix-aware KV caching; caching is keyed by org+project+route to avoid cross-tenant leakage. When you use shared models, we isolate KV caches per-tenant to prevent data bleed. There's an option to enable cross-tenant cache for performance but it's rarely recommended for regulated data.

[06:45] Samir: Quick note: some customers initially try to use one key for everything and hit isolation issues. We recommend a small set of project keys mapped to functional areas rather than a key per user.

[06:59] Evan: How fine-grained can RBAC be around keys?

[07:05] Leah: RBAC integrates with SSO; roles can be scoped to projects, and you can create API keys that inherit role limits. For example, a key can be read-only for model configs but still allow inference.

[07:20] Carlos: Show us an example of a complex policy — like mix of concurrency, priority and fairshare?

[07:26] Leah: Sure. I'll load a sample policy: name = "search-critical"; scope = project key "search"; reserved_slots = 4 on dedicated-pool-A; concurrency = 6; tokens_per_min = 8k; priority = high; fallback = degrade to "search-medium" model on hosted, and if cost > X switch to queued mode.

[07:49] Leah: Notice in the console the metrics panel — it simulates how the policy behaves under load and shows which requests would be throttled in red. There are some mislabels in the preview graphs sometimes — that's a small UX bug we've flagged.

[08:05] Carlos: That's helpful. Regarding quotas and billing, can we limit by dollar spend per project?

[08:12] Samir: Yes, you can set spend caps and attach alerts and programmatic webhooks when thresholds are hit. Those webhooks can trigger internal workflows to shut down keys or shift traffic.

[08:25] Marta: About compliance — if we route logs to our S3, how do you avoid PII in telemetry?

[08:32] Leah: We support redaction rules and metadata-only logging. You can strip request bodies before logs leave your VPC. For hosted customers we provide best-effort redaction but for strict compliance we recommend Private deployment.

[08:48] Evan: Question on performance: what p99 latencies do you typically see for dedicated pools versus hosted?

[08:54] Leah: For similar GPUs, dedicated pools can hit p99 latencies under 150ms for short responses (<128 tokens) depending on model and batching. Hosted has more variability due to multi-tenant batching but p50/p90 are often comparable; p99 can be higher. We'll provide benchmark artifacts.

[09:15] Carlos: Ok that clarifies. Can we do an A/B where we compare cost and latency across two policies?

[09:21] Samir: Yes — Redwood Optimize can run synthetic workloads and estimate cost/latency tradeoffs; we'll run it in the pilot.

[09:30] Priya: If we want to run an internal load test, how do we simulate sticky routing?

[09:36] Leah: We'll provide a load test harness—scripts that exercise multiple keys and can simulate warm KV caches, cold starts, and spikes. I'll drop a link after the call.

[09:47] Evan: Any gotchas for using BYOK with KMS? We've done that with other vendors and it's sometimes tricky.

[09:53] Samir: There's a one-time key rotation and permissions step. For Private we mount your KMS; for Hosted enterprise we set up a dedicated encryption key for your org. We'll send the integration checklist.

[10:05] Carlos: On the topic of routing — do you allow region-based routing rules for EU-only traffic?

[10:11] Leah: Yes — you can create region guards. Policies can include region constraints; traffic from EU can only be routed to EU pools. That also applies to model variants if you host data-resident models.

[10:25] Marta: Legal follow-up — who retains control of keys in hosted?

[10:29] Samir: In hosted with Redwood-managed KMS, Redwood manages the key but we can provide dedicated keys per customer under enterprise terms. For full control you would do Private or VPC.

[10:39] Priya: Let's move to pilot scope.

[10:42] Samir: Proposed pilot: 2 weeks, dedicated pool sized based on your traffic, run a smoke and stress test, measure p99 and cost per 1k tokens, validate failover and audit logging. We provision routes for 3 project keys (search, chat, embeddings).

[10:56] Carlos: That sounds good. What's the cost/commit? We want predictable monthly cost for pilot.

[11:02] Samir: For a 2-week pilot we usually offer trial credits and temporary capacity; we'll provide an estimate based on your profile. No long-term commit required to run the pilot.

[11:13] Evan: How does billing for dedicated work after pilot? Is it a flat reserved commit?

[11:18] Samir: Yes — Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly/annual pricing. You can add burst capacity on top. There are also hybrid patterns where some capacity is reserved and the rest is on-demand.

[11:29] Priya: For throttles — can we configure per-API endpoint rate limits (e.g., 60 reqs/min for /generate-chat) rather than token-based?

[11:37] Leah: Yes, the policy engine supports both token and request-count limits per route. Request-count is useful for endpoints with long but similar token counts.

[11:48] Carlos: Any examples of customers using dynamic quotas that change by time of day?

[11:54] Leah: Yes, we have time-windowed policies — e.g., higher quotas in off-peak hours for batch jobs, and stricter during business hours. The console has a schedule editor.

[12:06] Evan: For fallback model variants — is quality monitored automatically when fallback occurs?

[12:12] Leah: There's an eval hook — if fallback triggers, Redwood Optimize can run a prompt set and measure quality delta. You can set a threshold that triggers rollback or notification.

[12:23] Carlos: On the SDK side, any client changes for org/project key model selection?

[12:29] Leah: Minimal. You supply the API key and optionally override route preferences. The SDK will surface a header for project key. No major integration.

[12:39] Priya: A couple of small gotchas we ran into in the past: key rotation causing in-flight failures, and rate-limiter edge cases where burst tokens depleted unexpectedly. How do you mitigate?

[12:50] Samir: Best practices include rolling key rotations, short-lived tokens for clients, and monitoring for token-bucket exhaustion. For burst variance we recommend reserved slots for critical routes.

[13:03] Marta: Re legal — can audit logs be redacted automatically before delivery?

[13:09] Leah: Yes, redaction rules can be applied to logs and you can choose metadata-only export. We'll include the config example.

[13:18] Carlos: Will you share a sample policy playbook with examples for search, chat, and embeddings?

[13:23] Samir: Yes — action item: we'll send a playbook with sample configs and recommended defaults.

[13:30] Priya: Okay, anything else we should cover?

[13:33] Evan: Maybe quick demo of the API quota override endpoint?

[13:37] Leah: Sure — quick snippet: POST /orgs/:org/keys/:key/policy with JSON body. It returns a policy ID and the new policy is active within seconds. Sorry there's a typo in the playground snippet, ignore the extra comma.

[13:53] Carlos: Could you show a live sample where a route is throttled and fallback occurs?

[13:58] Leah: Yep — I'll run a synthetic spike. (sounds of keys clacking) Simulating 2k concurrent requests to search-critical... you can see the metrics spike, tokens cross threshold, fairness algorithm starts redirecting a subset to hosted fallback — red lines are throttled requests.

[14:20] Priya: I see some 429s. Do you expose the reason code so our clients can react differently?

[14:27] Leah: Yes, error codes are fine-grained: 429.rate_limit, 429.concurrency_limit, 429.org_quota_exceeded, etc. We recommend handling 429.rate_limit with exponential backoff, and 429.org_quota_exceeded to trigger admin alerts.

[14:43] Carlos: Great. For the pilot, can we collect a p99 breakdown by route and key?

[14:49] Samir: Yes dashboards include per-key latency percentiles and cost breakdowns. We'll set up a shared dashboard for your team.

[14:59] Marta: Final legal note — we might need a Data Processing Agreement.

[15:04] Samir: We'll send the DPA template and engage legal as needed.

[15:09] Carlos: Okay, let's recap next steps.

[15:12] Samir: Recap: Samir send playbook and SOC2/security artifacts; Leah provision trial capacity and load test plan; Carlos provide traffic profile and region constraints; Marta return DPA and SOC2 answers. Schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2026-03-09.

[15:29] Evan: Sounds good. One last thing — do you support on-prem private deployments for EU-only data?

[15:36] Leah: Yes, Private deployments and VPC options are supported; we can do an on-prem package if required though that is a longer engagement.

[15:45] Carlos: Great, thanks everyone. That was super helpful.

[15:48] Samir: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the items.

[15:52] (call ends)

Notes: transcription has occasional mislabels and minor pauses. References to internal artifacts: "org vs project key playbook" (link to be shared), "pilot load test harness" (link to be shared), "SOC2 artifact pack" (link to be shared).
